method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Common and benign**: it affects the cosmetic appearance of the head and **does not cause developmental delay.**
claims.source_text: Common, benign condition that affects the cosmetic appearance of an infant’s head. Does not cause developmental delay
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No imaging is required**: diagnose on history and examination, including the absence of craniosynostosis features. Cranial X-ray or CT is not needed to confirm plagiocephaly or brachycephaly.
claims.source_text: Imaging is not required, diagnosis is based on history and examination findings including the absence of features of craniosynostosis … Imaging (eg cranial X-ray or CT scan) not required to confirm plagiocephaly or brachycephaly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for a co-existing tight sternocleidomastoid** (congenital muscular torticollis) and other risk factors.
claims.source_text: Assessment includes identifying the presence of a co-existing tight sternocleidomastoid muscle (congenital muscular torticollis) and other risk factors
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most resolve without treatment**, improving with counterpositioning and physiotherapy.
claims.source_text: Most resolve without any treatment and will show improvement with counterpositioning measures and physiotherapy intervention
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Positional plagiocephaly** = posterior flattening on one side, possibly with ear misalignment and facial asymmetry. **Brachycephaly** = symmetrical occipital flattening and widening, often co-existing. **Scaphocephaly** = long narrow skull flattened on both sides.
claims.source_text: Skull deformation involving posterior flattening of either side of the head. This may result in ear misalignment and facial asymmetry … Brachycephaly: symmetrical occipital flattening and widening of the head, which often co-exists with positional plagiocephaly … Scaphocephaly: elongated narrow skull with flattening on both sides of the head, occipital bulge and frontal bossing
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Caused by external moulding** from lying on the back or a one-sided posture preference. **Risk factors:** low tone, delayed gross motor development, minimal tummy time, tight SCM, developmental dysplasia of the hip.
claims.source_text: External moulding forces due to the infant lying on their back or unilateral posture preference … Risk factors low tone delayed gross motor development minimal tummy time tight sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle (congenital muscular torticollis) developmental dysplasia of the hip
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Over one third of infants** have plagiocephaly in the first few months; most **self-correct by the time they can sit unsupported**, driven by rapid cranial growth in the first 4–6 months (corrected age if premature).
claims.source_text: Over one third of infants have plagiocephaly in the first few months of life which improves once the infant can move their head independently … Most resolve without intervention (self-correction) by the time the infant can sit without support … Self-correction occurs because of the rapid cranial growth in the first 4-6 months of life (for premature infants use 4-6 months corrected age), and ongoing growth until the anterior fontanelle closes
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Plagiocephaly and brachycephaly persist in around 1% of teenagers.**
claims.source_text: Plagiocephaly and brachycephaly are present in around 1% of teenagers
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Craniosynostosis** = premature fusion of one or more sutures with **ridging**; it may affect brain development, **does not improve over time**, and can be syndromic (e.g. Apert, Crouzon).
claims.source_text: Craniofacial anomaly causing skull deformity which may be associated with abnormal brain development Caused by premature fusion of one or more skull sutures resulting in ridging of sutures Does not improve over time May be an isolated finding with a single suture involved, or may be associated with other syndromes eg Apert, Crouzon syndrome
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mimics:** unilateral coronal craniosynostosis (forehead flattening) and unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis (occipital flattening opposite the forehead protuberance).
claims.source_text: Unilateral coronal craniosynostosis (causes forehead flattening) Unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis (causes occipital flattening on the opposite side to the forehead protuberance)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Congenital muscular torticollis**, usually noted in the first month: head tilt toward the tight SCM, looking to the opposite side, plagiocephaly on the opposite side, sometimes a palpable SCM lump.
claims.source_text: Usually noted within the first month of life Clinical features head tilt toward the same side as the tight SCM muscle tendency to look to the opposite side of the tight SCM muscle plagiocephaly on the opposite side of the tight SCM muscle lump in the SCM muscle may be palpable
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Identify torticollis early and refer to a physiotherapist** — plagiocephaly improves once the tight SCM is treated. Also associated: reduced vision or nystagmus (head tilt to see more clearly) and cervical scoliosis, e.g. Klippel-Feil syndrome.
claims.source_text: Early identification and management including referral to physiotherapist is beneficial as plagiocephaly will improve once the tight SCM is treated … reduced vision and nystagmus result in head tilt to improve visual clarity Cervical scoliosis eg Klippel Feil syndrome
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Assess for plagiocephaly** with any of: head-turning preference, head tilt, one-sided posterior flattening (parents may report a bump on the 'normal' side), symmetrical occipital flattening, ear displacement, forehead asymmetry, facial asymmetry.
claims.source_text: Assess an infant for positional plagiocephaly if they present with one or more of the following Head turning preference to one side Head tilt Posterior flattening on one side of the head (though parents may report a bump/bulge on the opposite ‘normal’ side) Symmetrical occipital flattening (brachycephaly) Ear displacement Asymmetrical protuberance of the forehead Facial asymmetry (one eye appears smaller)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **History:** birth (breech, multiple) and gestation; one-sided looking preference awake and asleep; gross motor development and tolerance of tummy time; handling, sleeping, feeding and carrying positions; change in head shape over time.
claims.source_text: Birth history (breech, multiple birth) and gestational age Preference for looking to one side only during awake and asleep time … Gross motor development eg head control, tone, sitting supported, tolerance of tummy time Parent/carer preference in infant handling and positioning eg front or back sleeping, preferred feeding or carrying position Onset and change in head shape over time (worsening or improvement)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine from above**, infant on the parent's lap: a **parallelogram-shaped head**, frontal protuberance and forward ear on the side of the flattening, and a posterior bump on the opposite side support plagiocephaly.
claims.source_text: Place infant on parent’s lap with examiner standing at the infant’s back Observe head from above. Features which support a clinical diagnosis of plagiocephaly: parallelogram shape head frontal protuberance on same side as posterior flattening ear pushed forward on same side as posterior flattening posterior protuberance (‘bump’) on the opposite ‘normal’ side
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Palpate the anterior fontanelle:** closed in 1% at 3 months, 38% at 12 months and 96% at 24 months. **An open fontanelle predicts better response** to physiotherapy or helmet therapy.
claims.source_text: 1% have a closed fontanelle at 3 months of age, 38% at 12 months of age, 96% at 24 months of age The size of the anterior fontanelle is useful in predicting response to physiotherapy or helmet therapy. An infant with an open fontanelle has more capacity for cranial growth and re-modelling
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Feel for ridging of the coronal or sagittal sutures** (craniosynostosis), and check head circumference, eye movements, back and spine, and neurology.
claims.source_text: Features of craniosynostosis: ridging of coronal or sagittal sutures Other: head circumference, eye movements, back and spine, and neurological examination to exclude other conditions associated with plagiocephaly
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **If craniosynostosis is suspected, refer urgently to a craniofacial service**, which decides on imaging.
claims.source_text: If craniosynostosis is suspected, refer urgently to a craniofacial service that can decide on optimal diagnostic imaging
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not use any pillow during sleep** to prevent or treat flattening — **risk of sudden infant death syndrome.**
claims.source_text: Do not use any pillow during sleep to prevent or manage flattening due to the risk of sudden infant death syndrome
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Counterpositioning:** reduce time on the flat side by arranging the environment so the infant turns toward the opposite side.
claims.source_text: Reducing the amount of time the infant spends lying on the flat side of their head will help improve the head shape … Counterpositioning promotes active positioning of the head towards the opposite side of the flattening, by organising the environment so the infant is encouraged to turn towards that side
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Example, right-sided plagiocephaly:** move the cot so the infant looks left when a carer enters; lay on the left side or back with toys on the left; carry to encourage turning left. **Regular tummy time** builds neck strength and head control.
claims.source_text: Change the position of the cot so the infant looks to the left when the parent/caregiver enters the room Awake time Lay the infant on their left shoulder/side and place toys in front Lay the infant on their back and place toys on their left side Regular tummy time strengthens the muscles of the neck and helps develop head control Carry the infant in a position which encourages head turning to the left
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Physiotherapy:** parent education, handling and counterpositioning advice, and — for congenital muscular torticollis — passive stretching and strengthening of the opposite SCM; the physiotherapist also monitors progress and advises on specialist referral.
claims.source_text: A physiotherapist can provide parent education, recommendations for infant handling, counterpositioning as well as specific exercises if congenital torticollis is present. Exercises for congenital muscular torticollis include passive stretching and strengthening of the opposite SCM muscle A physiotherapist can monitor for improvement in head shape and provide guidance as to whether specialist referral is required
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Some evidence supports a helmet for severe deformity not improving** with counterpositioning and physiotherapy; **some residual deformity remains** even with a helmet.
claims.source_text: There is some evidence for benefit of the use of a helmet in infants with severe deformity that is not improving with counterpositioning and physiotherapy Even with helmet therapy there will be residual deformity of the skull
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Optimal timing is around 6–7 months**; infants with developmental delay or torticollis may qualify with less deformity. **Unlikely to help after 10 months.**
claims.source_text: Optimal timing is around 6-7 months of age. Children with developmental delay or torticollis can be considered for a helmet with less deformity as these children are less likely to self-correct over time (because they spend more time on the flat spot) Unlikely to benefit infants >10 months of age due to the slowing of skull growth and anterior fontanelle closure
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Custom-made by an orthotist and worn 23 hours a day**, for an average of 6 weeks to 3 months. For brachycephaly it prevents further widening but does not reverse it.
claims.source_text: For brachycephaly, it improves occipital growth and prevents further widening (it does not reverse it) Custom made and fitted by an orthotist. Worn 23 hours per day for an average duration of 6 weeks to 3 months, depending on the improvement in head shape
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severity scales** (e.g. 0 = no asymmetry to 3 = severe, per feature) guide referral and monitoring; **helmet thresholds vary — seek local specialist advice.**
claims.source_text: Severity assessment can be used to guide the need for referral to a specialist service and help monitor progress … Includes a score from 0 (no asymmetry) to 3 (severe asymmetry) in each of the clinical features … Scoring thresholds for consideration of helmet therapy may vary, seek local specialist advice
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer to a specialist clinic** (paediatrics or craniofacial) for: severe head shape worsening despite counterpositioning and physiotherapy · suspected craniosynostosis · congenital muscular torticollis not improving with community physiotherapy.
claims.source_text: Refer to specialist clinic (paediatrics or craniofacial service) when Infant with severe positional head shape, worsening with time and not responding to general measures eg counterpositioning, physiotherapy Infant with suspected craniosynostosis Infant with congenital muscular torticollis not improving with community physiotherapist
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Positional plagiocephaly' (Last updated January 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Positional_plagiocephaly/, retrieved 2026-09-23
